A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PA-Tool research. All pages, including appendices A–F in v1 and A–K in v2, are readable, with sufficient text, equations, tables, and figures for comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original MetaTool and RoTBench experiments, supervised fine-tuning comparisons, error analysis, and hyperparameter experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, API-Bank and τ-Bench evaluations, training-exposure experiments, and computational measurements.

M1.justification: The three core stages remain unchanged, but v2 extends the specified procedure with collision resolution: the highest-peakedness component locks a contested name, while others advance to alternative candidates until names are unique (Appendix I). v1 specifies no corresponding cross-component selection step.

E1.justification: v2 adds API-Bank Call and Retrieval+Call evaluations and τ-Bench Retail tasks (Section 6.5). These extend coverage to retrieving APIs before invocation and completing policy-governed customer-service tasks through user interaction and database modifications. MetaTool and clean RoTBench coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds MostFreq on both benchmarks and Human-designed schemas on MetaTool, retaining Base and Greedy. Tables 11–13 additionally evaluate BM25 correction, ToolLLM embedding correction, constrained decoding, and a target-model adaptation of EasyTool, including combinations with PA-Tool.

E3.justification: Reported RoTBench cases change from 175 to 105. Table 2 changes its MetaTool test-sample caption from 10% to 20%, matching the split already stated in v1’s appendix. v2 also replaces the stated one-shot, target-description inference setup with candidate-list/full-schema prompt descriptions. New designs include doubled-data SFT, additional model configurations up to 70B, all-token training for exposure analysis, and end-to-end database-state scoring. These disclosures do not establish reruns of retained results.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct testing of peakedness versus training exposure, combinations with other training-free approaches, doubled-data SFT and cross-domain degradation analysis, collision frequencies, runtime measurements, and τ-Bench error trajectories. The original error breakdown and hyperparameter study are retained; their relocation is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: v2 newly specifies five independent τ-Bench runs and reports their mean pass rate (Section 6.5 and Appendix D.4). v1 reports no comparable repeated-run aggregation. Neither version supplies confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for new tasks, comparators, models, and analyses. Among retained entries, Qwen2.5-7B PA-Tool’s RoTBench multi-turn tool-selection score changes from 18.6% to 35.7% in Table 1, although v2 Table 11 still gives 18.6%. Table 2’s PA-Tool Similar score changes from 72.2% to 72.7% alongside revised sample documentation. These are reported-value changes, not established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The threshold, peakedness, maximization, and tie-breaking definitions in Equations 1–4 remain unchanged, as does Algorithm 1. The new training-exposure experiment supplies empirical evidence rather than a new mathematical derivation or proof.

C1.justification: The central training-free schema-alignment contribution and headline 17-point improvement and 80% error reduction remain. v2’s introduction additionally claims experimentally validated exposure sensitivity, compatibility with several existing approaches, and end-to-end task-completion benefits. These extend the claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes that functional confusion and contextual understanding require capabilities beyond schema optimization; v2 interprets their reductions as indirect benefits from reduced cognitive load. It adds interpretations concerning catastrophic forgetting, complementary correction mechanisms, description-induced semantic drift, and model-capacity-dependent benefits. The limitations section replaces the original failure-mode qualification with a capacity-dependent discussion while retaining language and training-distribution caveats.

D1.justification: v2 adds detailed scoring rules and inference prompts, GPT-generated reasoning for SFT data, batch size 16, hardware and software specifications, timing information, and implementations of the additional comparison methods. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without necessarily establishing changes to previously undisclosed settings. Both versions still promise code release upon publication.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Qu et al.’s tool-learning survey, BM25, and Sweet-RL, and develops its relationship to retrieval, constrained decoding, and description enhancement. The original research positioning largely remains. The duplicated API-Bank bibliography entries represent the same previously cited work.

P1.justification: The introduction, method motivation, results narrative, and limitations undergo substantial rewriting and compression. Numbered results subsections become compact benchmark paragraphs, the hyperparameter discussion moves from the main analysis to Appendix J, and the appendices are extensively reorganized around protocols and additional analyses.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain substantial row or column structure, and v2 adds benchmark, comparator, runtime, and collision tables, a training-exposure plot, model-gain plots, and multiple prompt panels. The original hyperparameter plot is retained as Figure 15, with its numerical tables relocated and renumbered as Tables 7–9.

improvement.justification: v2 improves assessability through frequency and human controls, exposure testing, end-to-end evaluation, and previously missing protocol details. However, the conflicting scores in Tables 1 and 11, Figure 14’s RoTBench sums labeled as averages, and claims of consistently beneficial combinations despite regressions in Tables 12–13 weaken the expanded conclusions. These reporting problems limit the net quality gain.
